title: I'm testing a way to put LLM characters in a game: the model only acts, the game owns every fact. Papers, Please-style, playable in the browser
author: Aromatic-Being5180
selftext:
**The game:** you're a border inspector at a railway crossing in 2003. Travellers, the people you phone and the colleagues who email you are all LLM characters. You question them in your own words, check their story against documents, archives and phone records, then stamp ADMITTED, DENIED or DETAINED. A newspaper tells you what happened next. Six short levels, solo or co-op for 2–3 players, in English or Italian.

**Play it:** [https://valico-di-grest.github.io/border-pass-int/](https://valico-di-grest.github.io/border-pass-int/) (browser, free, no signup)

The video is real gameplay: the replies are live and unedited.

**The approach I'm testing: the LLM acts, the game directs**

* **The game owns every fact.** Documents, luggage, what's on the phone and what a character is allowed to do all live in the game data. The model only chooses the words, a facial expression and two mood values (stress and trust). It can't hand you a document unless its trust is high enough, it can't make phone calls, and it can't leave the counter: the engine decides all of that.
* **Secrets have explicit unlock conditions,** usually a specific piece of evidence plus the inspector actually connecting the dots. I tested them with scripted bluffs, threats, promises and jailbreak attempts: no early confession in about 90 tries on the hardest character.
* **Characters are written as a short voice card plus hand-written example exchanges for each kind of moment** (kind, rude, threatening, bluffing, showing evidence, pressing, off-topic). The game detects the moment and passes the matching examples. There are no lines to recite: when the sheets contained quoted lines, the model repeated them word for word.
* **A hidden "thought" before every reply:** what the inspector really means and what the character wants right now. The server strips it before anything reaches the browser. It was the single most useful change: in my tests, early secret leaks went from 10 to 0 and contradictions from 9 to 3.
* **A mix of two models to keep costs very low.** GPT-6 Luna, a very cheap model, plays most of the turns. Gemini 3.8 Flash steps in only at key moments: a character's first line, when you show evidence, accuse, bluff or put on pressure. That's about a third of the turns. A 30-level session costs about $0.50 in API calls, against about $1.20 with Gemini everywhere and about $0.15 with Luna alone. Luna alone felt noticeably flatter exactly at the moments that matter; in blind comparisons I preferred the mix 10 times out of 16.
* **Everything runs server-side.** The browser only sends IDs and what you type, and replies are signed, so the conversation history can't be forged.

**What I'd love to know** (answering by number is perfect)

1. Do the characters feel like people, or like an AI playing a part? Where did it break for you?
2. Did you catch a character inventing something the game didn't back up?
3. For this kind of game, is typing freely better than choosing from lines?
4. If you've built LLM characters yourself: how do you handle secrets, cost and repetition? Is there anything here you'd do differently?
5. Is this economically sustainable? At roughly $0.50 of API cost per full playthrough, how would you fund a game like this: free with a daily cap, a one-off price, a subscription, something else? As a player, would you pay for it knowing every conversation costs money to run?

There's a short anonymous survey at the end of each level. Harsh feedback is welcome.

I built it solo with Claude Code. The pixel art is drawn by code, not by image generators.

comments.author: jaykrown
comments.body:
much better, but remove the crossword minigame idea, it's feature creep and detracts from the main value of the game, which is character interaction.  
  
the face emotion is a nice touch, but if it's causing you too much time and complexity, i'd just remove it or simplify it as much as you can.  
  
also the entire system where you go to "computer" and type in the passport seems to detract from the fun of having to look at dates yourself.  
  
the phone system seems also like feature creep, unless you intend to use it to call officials/authorities to help determine some information?  
  
thanks for sharing, i look forward to the next update, sharing it through videos like that and with text information is massive to help you get more attention, keep that schedule

replies.author: Aromatic-Being5180
replies.body:
Thanks again for the feedback, this is really useful. I’m actually redesigning a few things right now to make the AI interaction much more central to the game, and to remove or simplify systems that distract from that core loop.

I agree that some of the secondary mechanics should probably be simplified or removed, so the experience stays focused on what actually makes the game interesting instead of spreading the player’s attention too much.

I’m also reconsidering the computer/passport flow and the phone. If they stay, I want them to support the interrogation directly rather than feel like separate systems.

Really appreciate you following the updates. The feedback is helping me understand much better what the strongest part of the game actually is.

replies.author: jaykrown
replies.body: You're welcome, you should be focusing on absolutely everything you can do it make it different than Papers, Please. Be inspired by the original game, but you have the opportunity to make it better. The more you copy Papers, Please the less value your game will have in the long term.
